actions.text:
CMatrixLab
by Martin Grossman
martin.grossman@gmail.com
Generic ML
Simple view
Reset ↺

Your flu test is positive. What’s the chance you really have flu? That’s precision—and it also depends on how common flu is among the people tested.
Compare 10% and 50% sick using the same test. Precision changes, even though the portion of sick people correctly testing positive (TPR) and the portion of people without flu getting a false alarm (FPR) stay the same.

A CLOSER LOOK

From a result to a probability
Simple view
The basics
Formulas
Bayes
A positive test is a clue, not the final answer.

Actual tells us whether a person really has flu; the test predicts positive (+) or negative (−). Even an accurate test can produce many false alarms when flu is rare.

Explore the Bayes breakdown →

Four possible outcomes
1,000 weighted people
TP · 480
Flu detected: flu, test +
FP · 20
False alarm: no flu, test +
FN · 20
Flu missed: flu, test −
TN · 480
Correctly cleared: no flu, test −

Why balance matters. When flu is more common, more positive tests come from people who really have flu.

With the signal sensitivity and score separation fixed, changing the sick portion changes Precision while TPR and FPR stay fixed wherever both rates are defined.

How this demonstration works

1,000 weighted people. Counts are expected values and may be fractional. Sick portion changes counts and precision; TPR and FPR stay fixed at the same signal sensitivity and score separation.
